title: Contextualized Privacy Defense for LLM Agents
claim: Static prompting and blocking guards either leak data or lose helpfulness; step-specific proactive guidance achieves both privacy and utility.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: trajectory, defenses, outcomes; color-coded result boxes with scores
description: A three-column diagram with dashed borders: Agent Trajectory on the left, Defenses in the middle, Action Evaluation on the right. The left column is a stack of blue message boxes showing an agent's steps: a system prompt, reading messages, Mike's request for the meeting time and Emily's ID number (the ID is in red), the agent's reply, and 'Success!'. The middle column has three green boxes: Prompting, CDI (Ours) and Guarding. Each holds a short example of that defense's instruction or message, and key phrases are highlighted in green or red. Arrows lead from each defense to an outcome box on the right. The Prompting outcome is red: it leaks the ID. The CDI outcome is green: it shares the meeting time and refuses the ID. The Guarding outcome is gray: it refuses everything. Each outcome box has a score label (PP, HS, AD). The eye goes first to the red, green and gray outcome boxes.
caption: Illustration of different privacy defenses. Emily (data subject) sends David (data sender, Emily's assistant) the meeting time and her ID number. Mike (data recipient, Emily's subordinate) requests both items, but he is only entitled to the meeting time. Prompting prepends privacy-enhancing instructions to the agent's system prompt. It provides no context-specific instructions, so it remains vulnerable to diverse attacks. Guarding uses a separate guard model to screen the proposed action for potential privacy violations. However, it only blocks sensitive data without offering rewrite suggestions, resulting in reduced helpfulness. Contextualized Defense Instructing (CDI) employs a separate instructor model to generate guidance before each action. By providing proactive, context-aware privacy guidance, it achieves the best trade-off between privacy and helpfulness.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on users' personal information, yet existing privacy defenses remain limited in both design and adaptability. Most prior approaches rely on static or passive defenses, such as prompting and guarding. These paradigms are insufficient for supporting contextual, proactive privacy decisions in multi-step agent execution. We propose Contextualized Defense Instructing (CDI), a new privacy defense paradigm in which an instructor model generates step-specific, context-aware privacy guidance during execution, proactively shaping actions rather than merely constraining or vetoing them. Crucially, CDI is paired with an experience-driven optimization framework that trains the instructor via reinforcement learning (RL), where we convert failure trajectories with privacy violations into learning environments. We formalize baseline defenses and CDI as distinct intervention points in a canonical agent loop, and compare their privacy-helpfulness trade-offs within a unified simulation framework. Results show that our CDI consistently achieves a better balance between privacy preservation (94.2%) and helpfulness (80.6%) than baselines, with superior robustness to adversarial conditions and generalization.
